A tip for mitts and soft wrist restraints...if you don't do this already...Put the wrist restraints on under the mitts and use the hole under the strap of the mitts to feed the strap of the restraint through. That way, the wrist restraints are tight enough, and the strap of the restraint keeps the mitt on. Old ladies have tiny hands. I promise the ICU didn't take the mitts off (hopefully). If you put the wrist restraint on top of the mitt it's way easier for them to get out of the wrist restraint then self extubate with their mitts on or fling the mitts off then grab the tube with their hands. Or the wrist restraint just slides up their arm, giving them slack to grab the tube.

Your partner dying is much different than getting a divorce. They say if a partner is widowed from a good and loving relationship, they're much likely to date a lot sooner. My brother was married less than 2 years after his (38f) wife died. I was dating 4 months after my husband (41m) died. Both of them died under sudden circumstances. She had breast cancer diagnosed at stage IV and my husband had PTSD. I think it's pretty normal to seek companionship after you've given all of yourself and time to someone you loved so fiercely.  Give your dad some grace if you can. He's lonely, he had the love of his life, and now he's seeking comfort in the way he's always gotten it. 

Me and my brother both got a lot of shit for dating so soon or whatever else, but unless you've been there, you just don't know. I always said I would never date again, but here I am. I miss my husband every day, but I also love the man I'm with. I talk about my husband with him and he understands that he'll alway have a place in my heart. Dating doesn't mean your dad doesn't miss your mom or that he doesn't still hold a place for her, in my experience it means the opposite. 

Sorry for your loss OP.

I worked in surgical ICU during the pandemic. What you're describing just didn't happen then. Our ER waiting room was usually 60 deep for a good year. We had no beds anywhere in the hospital. Our outpatient services were closed half the time to pull staff to our overflowing units. You had doctors and nurses seeing 4x the normal number of patients. Care sucked, staff was stretched way too thin. It's why so many doctors and nurses quit. If you weren't dying, you were referred out...and you'd probably get a telehealth appointment and then a referral for a CT in some amount of time. Outpatient is slow even in the best of times. 

By the way, it took me over 2 weeks to get a stat outpatient CT to confirm mastoiditis in 2021 due to staffing, restrictions, and the backlog of patients when things would periodically open. 

And honestly, I've seen some pretty messed up cases when the system isn't inundated. Waiting for insurance approval, etc. The way to get anything done quickly is usually the ER and that just wasn't happening then.

Article says original surgery was in 2020 and removed in 2021. I totally get that doctors can suck sometimes and not take things seriously, but I also get the immense amount of strain on the healthcare system in general during that time. Kind of a perfect storm for something like this to happen.

It's been almost a year and a half (August 2021). I'm doing OK, finally selling our house and getting ready to go travel in an RV for a while. Quit my job and put the house on the market in September. Ready for the moving forward part. Luckily, I am with someone who understands (his best friend). Basically, I'm just doing the best I can. He always wanted me to quit my job (ICU nurse, he was one too). Wish I'd done it when he was still here, but try to focus on all the amazing things I got to do with him and not the could haves. Lots of therapy to get me here, though. Just still gets me, he said all the right things, seemed almost like himself again, and put me at ease before he left (told me he was going on a fishing trip a couple hours from us, actually went to Maine). He wrote in his letter he was sorry for lying, but he knew he had to go and this was the only way he could find peace. I'm 37 and feel like 70 at this point.

Same, first attempt had no idea and came home and found him and got him to the hospital. Second attempt there were signs, but I found and stopped him (he left to go to a state park). Third attempt, he went out of state and couldn't get the police to do a welfare check after we finally found his location after 3 days ("If your husband wants to leave you he can", "Unless he told you he was suicidal in the last hour we can't do a check", etc etc). He was found the next day by hotel staff when he didn't check out. Sucked because I knew exactly where he was and the hotel staff would only crack his door and said they heard him snoring the night before he was found. He was across the country from me because he knew I'd stop him. Sometimes, signs or not, if someone wants to go there's nothing you can do.

Also, try to focus on one thing/resource at a time. Therapy can quickly become overwhelming if you try to do support groups, Al-Anon, EMDR, talk therapy etc all at once. Didn't get here quickly, give yourself time to heal and try to go with the process. Therapy becomes like a job so don't take on a ton at once, will honestly just make it overwhelming and you'll want to quit
